units.source_excerpt: The driving force behind this paper is to develop a model which remedies this conflict. In our report, we identify two models for the sweet spot, each based on a different definition.
units.function: Turn a physical contradiction into a model-comparison objective.
units.reusable_pattern: Because {observation} conflicts with {baseline}, compare {models} under explicit {definitions}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not manufacture a conflict or imply that model comparison resolves it without evidence.

units.source_excerpt: While it does lack some sensitivity and is limited in its ability to precisely predict outcomes, we ultimately conclude that the Brody Model is the ideal method for an assessment of the interplay between power and sweet spot location.
units.function: Place a limitation immediately before the front-page conclusion.
units.reusable_pattern: Although {limitations}, the tested model supports {bounded_use} for {scope}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not retain the word ideal when the stated limitations block that judgment.

units.source_excerpt: The typical player, however, is more concerned with stepping into the batter's box and striking the ball as efficiently and as far as possible.
units.function: Translate a broad physics setting into the user's concrete performance question.
units.reusable_pattern: Move from {domain_context} to the concrete question faced by {user}: {decision_metric}.
prohibited_generalizations: Audience framing cannot replace a computable performance definition.

units.source_excerpt: Using the Brody Model we generate an equation to determine the sweet spot's location, apply it to corked and aluminum bats, and perform a sensitivity analysis on the variables involved.
units.function: Compress the model, scenario, and sensitivity branches into one method preview.
units.reusable_pattern: Preview {model_output}, its application to {scenarios}, and the {sensitivity_dimension} tested.
prohibited_generalizations: A preview must not imply that every named branch was independently validated.

units.source_excerpt: For the purposes of this paper, the sweet spot represents the spot on the thick part of the barrel where maximum power is transferred to the ball upon contact. The purpose of this investigation is to develop a model that explains this empirical phenomenon.
units.function: Operationalize an ambiguous term and connect it to the modeling goal.
units.reusable_pattern: For this analysis, {construct} denotes {criterion} under {conditions}; the model addresses {purpose}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not use a definition that the model cannot compute or observe.

units.source_excerpt: A similarly obscure phenomenon is the 'sweet spot' of a baseball bat, a concept intuitively understood by even the most junior players, but which is very difficult to define.
units.function: Use familiar experience to motivate a precise definition problem.
units.reusable_pattern: Although {term} is familiar to {audience}, its measurable meaning remains {gap}.
prohibited_generalizations: Familiarity is not empirical evidence for a selected definition.

units.source_excerpt: Additionally, we will attempt to investigate the effects of different parameters upon a bat-ball collision, specifically how they affect location and effectiveness of the sweet spot. Included in this investigation is an examination of the utility of 'corking' a bat, as well as an examination of the differences observed between the performances of wooden and aluminum bats.
units.function: Expand the central location question into parameter and material scenario branches.
units.reusable_pattern: After defining {primary_output}, examine how {parameters} and {scenarios} change it.
prohibited_generalizations: Listing a material scenario does not establish a material effect.

units.source_excerpt: Identify Objectives; Define Terms; State Assumptions; Develop Models; Sensitivity Analysis.
units.function: Expose the paper's work sequence before technical development.
units.reusable_pattern: Sequence {objectives}, {definitions}, {assumptions}, {models}, and {verification} before execution.
prohibited_generalizations: A roadmap is not evidence that each stage was completed.

units.source_excerpt: This report is produced with a baseball audience in mind. We want the average baseball enthusiast to be able to read our paper and gain some understanding of a few of baseball's fundamental questions: the sweet spot, the effects of corking, and effects of differences between bat materials.
units.function: Name the reader and the decisions the exposition must support.
units.reusable_pattern: Name {reader}, the required level of access, and the {questions} the report must answer.
prohibited_generalizations: Accessibility cannot excuse undefined variables or unsupported conclusions.

units.source_excerpt: To guide the presentation of our model, we have focused on four primary objectives: Answering the Problem; Simplicity and Clarity; Applicability; Resiliency.
units.function: Turn broad quality expectations into an explicit evaluation frame.
units.reusable_pattern: Evaluate {model} against declared criteria for {coverage}, {clarity}, {applicability}, and {resiliency}.
prohibited_generalizations: Criteria must be returned to with evidence, not only named.

units.source_excerpt: The center of percussion has historically been identified with the concept of the sweet spot for implements such as baseball bats and tennis rackets. When a force is applied at the COP no vibration is felt at the pivot point. Thus, the COP is often tied to the tactile feeling of the sweet spot, where the hitter feels little to no sting in his hands.
units.function: Separate a tactile construct from the later performance construct.
units.reusable_pattern: Define {candidate} through {physical_condition} and the observable {response} it represents.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not equate a comfort response with maximum performance.

units.source_excerpt: An alternate definition of the sweet spot is the strike location that yields maximum performance; this depends on the definition of maximum performance itself.
units.function: Make the objective-function dependency explicit before optimization.
units.reusable_pattern: If {construct} is an optimum, define the performance metric before locating {argmax}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not optimize an ambiguous label or conflate speed, energy, and restitution.

units.source_excerpt: The principle behind the COP relates to the interaction of rotational and translational motion caused by a ball striking a bat.
units.function: Introduce the two mechanisms before displaying the governing relation.
units.reusable_pattern: Before {equation}, name the competing mechanisms {mechanism_1} and {mechanism_2}.
prohibited_generalizations: A qualitative mechanism diagram is explanation, not validation.

units.source_excerpt: Alternatively, when the ball impacts at the COP, the rotational and translational forces acting on the handle cancel out. The collision feels smooth to the batter, and the lack of shock to the hands acts as an indicator that a solid hit has been made.
units.function: Connect force cancellation to the observable handle response.
units.reusable_pattern: At {location}, {mechanisms} cancel, producing the observable {indicator}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not infer maximum exit speed from handle-force cancellation.

units.source_excerpt: After investigating the COP as a possible location of maximum performance, we have determined that it is inadequate for our purposes, and another model is required.
units.function: Use a named failure of the baseline to motivate the next model.
units.reusable_pattern: After testing {baseline} against {criterion}, state the specific gap that requires {next_model}.
prohibited_generalizations: A replacement must address the named gap rather than merely add complexity.

units.source_excerpt: The derivation of this model stems from a combination of the three concepts below: Conservation of Linear Momentum; Conservation of Angular Momentum; Definition of Coefficient of Restitution.
units.function: Declare the three-equation physical closure before derivation.
units.reusable_pattern: Derive {response} by combining {balance_1}, {balance_2}, and {contact_law} in one frame.
prohibited_generalizations: The balances close only when velocities, axes, and inertia references are consistent.

units.source_excerpt: When a bat moves through space and comes into contact with a ball, both translational and rotational forces must be considered. As the bat is swung, it travels in an arc around a pivot point, which requires rotational motion to be taken into account. The baseball itself travels in a straight line, causing the bat to experience a translational force on impact, and so linear velocity also comes into play.
units.function: Explain why each term family belongs in the collision model.
units.reusable_pattern: Map each observed motion in {event} to the corresponding state or balance in {model}.
prohibited_generalizations: The explanation must use the same frame and point velocities as the equations.

units.source_excerpt: In order to find the maximum value of the function vf, it is necessary to take the first partial derivative with respect to b. At the maximum value the graph is neither increasing nor decreasing, so the first derivative will be 0.
units.function: Tie the derivative operation directly to the impact-location objective.
units.reusable_pattern: Differentiate {response} with respect to {decision_variable}, solve the stationary condition, then check roots and boundaries.
prohibited_generalizations: A zero derivative alone does not establish a feasible global maximum.

units.source_excerpt: If the final velocity of the ball was based on torque, then the location of the sweet spot should have been as far away from the pivot point as possible.
units.function: State the torque-only comparator as a falsifiable endpoint prediction.
units.reusable_pattern: Under {baseline_mechanism}, predict {boundary_outcome}; compare it with {full_model_output}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not claim that torque is invalid; state which omitted terms change the objective.

units.source_excerpt: Inserting these values in the COP equation, we found the location of the sweet spot to be at about 26.531 inches from the knob, or approximately 7.5 inches from the free end of the bat. While this distance is close to the expected values, it falls just outside the accepted 4-7 inches from the end of the bat.
units.function: Report the computed location in two field coordinates and compare it with a reference interval.
units.reusable_pattern: Report {result} in {coordinate_1} and {coordinate_2}, then compare it with {reference_range}.
prohibited_generalizations: Range proximity is a plausibility check, not predictive validation.

units.source_excerpt: The output dictates that b = 0.56557 m. Converting from meters to inches, this becomes 22.267 in. Moving this distance away from the axis of the moment of inertia, assumed to be 6 inches, indicates that the optimal location for hitting the ball exists 28.267 inches from the knob, which is about 5.733 inches from the free end.
units.function: Show each coordinate conversion between analytic output and field answer.
units.reusable_pattern: Convert {analytic_offset} through an explicit {coordinate_ledger} to the field-facing {answer}.
prohibited_generalizations: Every reference point and inertia axis in the conversion must be declared.

units.source_excerpt: Using Brody's Power Model, the value for the normal wooden bat remains bw = 0.56557, while the value of the corked bat is bc = 0.53847.
units.function: Place baseline and scenario location outputs in one direct comparison.
units.reusable_pattern: Under the shared {model}, compare {baseline_output} with {scenario_output}.
prohibited_generalizations: A parameter-bundle difference must not be labeled a structural material effect.

units.source_excerpt: For the normal wooden bat we find a final ball speed of 53.502 m/s, while the corked bat had a ball speed of 53.810 m/s. The nature of our assumptions precludes the results from being completely accurate under real world conditions.
units.function: Report paired scenario outputs and immediately attach an accuracy boundary.
units.reusable_pattern: Report {baseline} and {scenario} under {protocol}, then state the exact {validity_boundary}.
prohibited_generalizations: A caveat does not repair an undefined or circular result equation.

units.source_excerpt: The difference between the wooden bat and the aluminum bat exit speeds in this example is about .756 m/s. In English units, this is equivalent to 2.5 ft/s (1.7 MPH).
units.function: Express a scenario increment in SI and familiar field units.
units.reusable_pattern: State {difference} in {primary_unit} and translate it to {audience_unit} without changing the denominator.
prohibited_generalizations: Unit translation must not be used to imply an unmodeled safety effect.

units.source_excerpt: As the mass of the bat increases, so does the final speed of the ball. This graph may be misleading, however, in that the final speed is not very sensitive to the mass of the bat. This is only the case when the mass changes independent of the other variables, which is rarely the case.
units.function: Report a plotted direction, its small magnitude, and the fixed-factor boundary together.
units.reusable_pattern: Under {fixed_factor_protocol}, {output} moves {direction}; the magnitude is {size}, and {coupling} limits interpretation.
prohibited_generalizations: One-factor direction does not rank coupled design variables.

units.source_excerpt: If the thick portion of the barrel is hollowed with an approximately half inch diameter hole and filled with a less dense and more elastic material, such as cork or bouncy balls, the bat is rendered considerably lighter, which allows for a faster swing. One of the problems with hollowing out a bat is that the structural strength becomes compromised.
units.function: Introduce the modification through geometry, material, performance pathway, and structural tradeoff.
units.reusable_pattern: Describe {modification}, trace its {performance_pathway}, and retain the competing {tradeoff}.
prohibited_generalizations: A qualitative pathway must not be presented as a calibrated structural model.

units.source_excerpt: When a bat is corked, several changes take place. First, the mass of the bat decreases at the free end because the material used to fill the barrel is less dense than the wood of the bat itself. This translates into a lower moment of inertia. The combination of a lower moment of inertia and less weight in the bat results in a faster swing, given that the same amount of force is present.
units.function: Build the cork scenario as an explicit causal parameter chain.
units.reusable_pattern: Map {modification} to {mass_change}, {inertia_change}, and the assumed {human_response}.
prohibited_generalizations: The human-response link requires measurement or sensitivity, not assertion alone.

units.source_excerpt: The bat is treated as a solid mass that undergoes a perfect elastic collision with the ball. However, when corking a baseball bat, a certain amount of energy is lost to the material encased inside the wood. This energy loss is not included within the model.
units.function: Name the omitted mechanism and its direction relative to the computed scenario.
units.reusable_pattern: State {baseline_assumption}, identify omitted {mechanism}, and delimit the affected {output}.
prohibited_generalizations: An omitted mechanism's sign cannot be used to reverse a result without quantification.

units.source_excerpt: The difference between aluminum and wooden bats is modeled under the Brody Power Model following the same logic as our investigation of corking. We begin with our assumptions of the specific parameters for an aluminum bat: mass, moment of inertia, and angular velocity.
units.function: Declare reuse of the base model and enumerate the changed scenario inputs.
units.reusable_pattern: Reuse {base_model} while declaring every changed scenario input: {parameter_bundle}.
prohibited_generalizations: A changed parameter bundle does not isolate construction material.

units.source_excerpt: While the Brody Power Model indicates that the aluminum bat has elevated performance at its position of maximum power, it does not accurately depict the degree to which this performance increases. This is due to the fact that the model does not take into account a unique behavior exhibited by aluminum bats known as the trampoline effect.
units.function: Attach the omitted compliance mechanism to the numerical comparison's scope.
units.reusable_pattern: Retain {directional_result} while withholding {magnitude_claim} because {mechanism} is omitted.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not add an unmodeled trampoline effect numerically or causally to the reported result.

units.source_excerpt: We referenced a table for the wood and aluminum bats, which included relevant specifications for our equations. Since mass and moment of inertia are interconnected, this ensured that combinations of the two variables reflect true properties of the different bats. In the case of the corked bat, we researched sources which identified the reduction of mass by 2 oz when a bat is corked. We then made reasonable assumptions about the resulting change in the moment of inertia.
units.function: Separate sourced coupled inputs from the remaining assumed cork inertia.
units.reusable_pattern: For each input bundle, distinguish {sourced_values} from {assumed_values} and retain their coupling.
prohibited_generalizations: Reasonable must not substitute for a value, range, source, or sensitivity test.

units.source_excerpt: With the reasoning behind our assumptions in mind, we can now examine the sensitivity of the model to each variable. The only variables not included in this section are the mass of the ball and the location of optimal ball exit speed. The ball mass is not included because the range of possible masses is so narrow that for our purposes it does not vary. The value for the distance is not included because distance is completely dependent on the interplay of the other values.
units.function: Declare the varied set and justify two exclusions before plotting.
units.reusable_pattern: Before {sensitivity}, list varied inputs, fixed inputs, excluded quantities, and each exclusion rationale.
prohibited_generalizations: An excluded dependent output must still be traced through the response calculation.

units.source_excerpt: Using the specifications of the wooden bat as a baseline, we plotted a three-dimensional graph of the location on a bat that would be produced for a wide range of initial ball velocities and angular bat speeds. We then created a second plot which used the same model but added two constraints.
units.function: Move from an unconstrained two-input response surface to a constrained operating region.
units.reusable_pattern: Plot {response} over {input_1} and {input_2}, then overlay declared {constraints}.
prohibited_generalizations: A constraint based on the accepted answer cannot serve as independent validation.

units.source_excerpt: We then replaced each of the values one at a time with a variable to see how the final velocity changed as that variable changed.
units.function: State the one-at-a-time perturbation protocol in one sentence.
units.reusable_pattern: From {baseline}, vary one {input} at a time while holding {others} fixed and record {response}.
prohibited_generalizations: Label this as local one-factor sensitivity, not global robustness.

units.source_excerpt: Since the relation of bat speed to final ball speed is stronger than that of moment of inertia, the slight increase in speed caused by increasing the moment of inertia would be masked by the resulting decrease in swing speed. By only isolating one variable at a time, we are unable to discover which variable is more important towards increasing final ball speed.
units.function: Use the observed coupling to limit variable-importance claims from local plots.
units.reusable_pattern: When {inputs} are coupled, report the competing pathways and withhold {importance_ranking} from one-factor plots.
prohibited_generalizations: A local slope comparison does not identify a causal or globally important variable.

units.source_excerpt: Before producing our model, we laid out a set of four primary objectives which we intended to use to guide and bracket our investigation: Answering the Problem; Simplicity and Clarity; Applicability; Resiliency.
units.function: Reopen the conclusion with the declared evaluation contract.
units.reusable_pattern: Return to the declared criteria {criteria} before synthesizing {results}.
prohibited_generalizations: A criteria return must distinguish demonstrated results from self-assessment.

units.source_excerpt: Example I shows that the COP is capable of predicting the sweet spot in terms of 'feel,' but is unable to document the sweet spot in terms of maximum performance. Instead, we were forced to draw on the Brody Power Model in order to optimize this variable.
units.function: Close the baseline comparison by matching each model to its construct.
units.reusable_pattern: Use {baseline} for {bounded_construct}; use {replacement} for the unmet {objective}.
prohibited_generalizations: Do not call either model predictive beyond the evidence supporting its construct.

units.source_excerpt: When the assumptions are varied to predict the outcome of using a corked bat, a .31 m/s increase in ball exit speed is yielded. This constitutes a negligible enhancement of the sweet spot effect, and is subject to factors that might further mitigate this increase.
units.function: Answer the cork branch with an increment, interpretation, and omitted-factor boundary.
units.reusable_pattern: Under {scenario_assumptions}, report {increment}, interpret its decision scale, and retain {omitted_factors}.
prohibited_generalizations: The increment inherits the exit-speed equation's closure limits and cannot establish policy causation.

units.source_excerpt: Because changes in each variable were evaluated separately, however, we are unable to tell which variables carry a stronger correlation with changes in batted ball performance. Although the variables cannot be isolated, the model is able to take a given set of circumstances and predict the relative performances of two bats.
units.function: End the sensitivity branch by withholding rankings while retaining a conditional comparison use.
units.reusable_pattern: Because {protocol_limit}, withhold {ranking}; retain only the conditional {comparison_use}.
prohibited_generalizations: A conditional comparison still requires a closed equation and identified inputs.

units.source_excerpt: Laboratory research which produced empirical data for use specifically as our parameters would provide us with more accurate inputs, instead of relying on our assumptions. Laboratory research would help to confirm the results of our model's predictions to provide feedback in improving the model.
units.function: Translate parameter and validation gaps into a concrete experimental next step.
units.reusable_pattern: Collect {experimental_data} to identify {parameters}, test {predictions}, and revise {model}.
prohibited_generalizations: Future experiments must separate calibration data from held-out validation.
